name: LM2937IMPX-3.3_NOPB
title: LM2937: 500 mA low-dropout positive regulator, fixed 2.5 to 15 V, in TO-220, DDPAK/TO-263 and SOT-223
summary: A three-terminal fixed positive regulator with a PNP pass device, rated for 500 mA (400 mA in SOT-223) with about 0.5 V dropout at full load. Output is trimmed to 5 % across load, line and temperature, and the part is stable with output capacitor ESR up to 3 Ω. Built for automotive rails, it withstands reverse battery, 60 V input transients and −50 V reverse transients, and has current limiting, thermal shutdown and overvoltage shutdown near 32 V. LM2937IMPX-3.3/NOPB is the 3.3 V part in SOT-223 on a 2000-piece reel, rated for −40 to 85°C junction.

circuits.title: Figure 18. Typical application
circuits.description: The regulator between an unregulated input and the regulated output, with 0.1 µF from VIN to ground and 10 µF from VOUT to ground; GND carries the quiescent current IQ to ground. The output capacitor keeps the loop stable: at least 10 µF over the whole operating temperature range, ESR up to 3 Ω, mounted as near the regulator as possible. The input capacitor is needed only when the regulator sits more than 3 inches from the supply's filter capacitors.

operation.text: A fixed-output positive linear regulator for loads to 500 mA, built round a PNP pass transistor so the input can come within about 0.5 V of the output at full load (1 V at most across temperature). Output voltages are 2.5, 3.3, 5, 8, 10, 12 and 15 V, trimmed to 5 % over all operating conditions, in TO-220, DDPAK/TO-263 and SOT-223. Named uses are automotive, industrial control and point-of-load supplies.

The ground current is held to about 10 mA at a full 500 mA load once the input sits more than 3 V above the output; at 5 mA load it is about 2 mA. It rises sharply while the part is in dropout (Figure 5).

The regulator protects itself and the circuit it feeds against a reversed battery, a two-battery jump start and load-dump transients up to +60 V and −50 V. It is also protected against mirror-image insertion.
Above roughly 32 V on the input the output switches off. Performance is not guaranteed above 26 V, and running continuously above 26 V is to be avoided.
Output current is limited when the load resistance is very low, a dead short to ground included. Held at the limit, the part normally heats until thermal shutdown takes over.

The die switches off at about 150°C to ride out brief thermal overloads. It does not replace proper heat sinking: running at shutdown for long periods can shorten the part's life, since the junction is then beyond its absolute maximum.

There is no enable pin and no undervoltage lockout. Below VOUT + 1 V on the input the output follows the input; above it the output is regulated, though still sensitive to small input disturbances. With at least 2 V of headroom the dynamic response is better, so a supply of VOUT + 2 V or more keeps the output well regulated.

The output needs at least 10 µF for stability, with ESR between 10 mΩ and 3 Ω, and both must hold over the whole ambient temperature range. There is no upper limit on capacitance; more of it improves transient response. ESR outside the stable region (Figure 19) lets the loop oscillate. The upper ESR limit is 3 Ω from about 50 mA to 500 mA and rises to about 8 Ω toward zero load current.

Capacitor ESR is usually specified only at room temperature, so it must be checked over the full temperature range. An aluminium electrolytic's ESR rises about thirty times between 25°C and −40°C, making it a poor choice for cold operation. Solid tantalum holds its ESR better over temperature but costs more. One economical arrangement puts an aluminium and a tantalum capacitor in parallel, roughly 75 % of the capacitance in the aluminium part and 25 % in the tantalum; the tantalum's steadier ESR slows the rise of the combined ESR in the cold.

The supply should run from at least VOUT + 1 V to no more than 26 V, well regulated and clean. A capacitor on INPUT may be left off when the bulk filter capacitors of the supply are within three inches of the pin; fitting one does no harm.

Work out PD, then the allowed temperature rise TR(max), then the largest RθJA the design can stand. If that is at least 53°C/W (TO-220), 80°C/W (DDPAK/TO-263) or 174°C/W (SOT-223), the package alone is enough; otherwise it needs a heat sink. A TO-220 can go on a bought heat sink, sized with RθHA, or onto a copper plane on the board, where it behaves like the DDPAK/TO-263.

The DDPAK/TO-263 and SOT-223 are cooled through a copper plane on the board, with the tab soldered to it. On 1 oz copper without solder mask over the heat-sink area, the DDPAK/TO-263's RθJA falls with area but barely improves past one square inch, bottoming out at 32°C/W. Its derating curve assumes 35°C/W and a 125°C junction. The SOT-223 curves assume 74°C/W on 1 oz copper and 51°C/W on 2 oz copper, with an 85°C junction.
The tab is bonded inside to GND (pin 2). Solder it to a large copper area for cooling, and tie it to ground or leave it unconnected; it must never go to any other potential.
Hand soldering and wave soldering are not advised for the SOT-223: the heat can crack the package. Vapour phase or infrared reflow are the methods to use.

Board layout sets the part's PSRR, noise and transient behaviour. CIN and COUT go on the same side of the board as the regulator, as near the package as possible, each returned to the GND pin by a short, wide trace. Long or narrow traces and vias in these paths add inductance and resistance that hurt performance, worst during transients. On the SOT-223 layout, CIN bridges the INPUT copper at pin 1 and COUT the OUTPUT copper at pin 3 to the ground copper round the tab, and pin 2 runs down to a ground pour below.
Built-in ESD protection is limited: store and handle the parts with leads shorted or in conductive foam.
